questions.q: Why not run a standard statistical test on each feature every day?
questions.a: At production volumes it fires on harmless changes. Breck et al. (SysML 2019) mixed 0.01% noise into 100 million values and ran a chi-square test, a standard check of whether two distributions match: it raised a needless alert in 7 of 10 trials. They use the largest change in any one value's share instead, with thresholds like “allow changes of only up to 1% for each value”.

teach.title: How it works: why it hides, and the checks that find it

questions.q: The model is retrained daily on its own logged traffic. Does that make it worse?
questions.a: Yes, if the bug runs for days: in Breck et al.'s −1 example, served data becomes the next day's training data, so the bad values carry into the next model too. Retrain without the affected days once the feature is fixed (our reasoning). It's the same loop as a recommender learning from clicks it caused (Q50).

teach.title: How it works: why it hides, and the checks that find it

questions.q: How fresh does each feature need to be?
questions.a: Measure it. Rules of ML, Rule #8, asks how much quality drops with a model a day, a week or a quarter old; the ML Test Score suggests a small A/B test with older models to draw an age-against-quality curve. Do the same for each feature table, then set its age alert from the curve (our extension).

teach.title: How it works: why it hides, and the checks that find it

questions.q: Why can a model service show full uptime and no errors while its predictions are wrong?
questions.a: Service checks test that it answered, not what it answered from. A feature job that stops updating, or a lookup that falls back to a default, raises no error; the model scores stale or empty inputs.

questions.q: What does Google's Rules of ML report about a stale table at Play?
questions.a: Rule #10 says Play once had a table stale for six months, and refreshing it alone raised install rate by 2%; stopped tables make systems decay gradually rather than fail.

teach.title: How it works: why it hides, and the checks that find it

questions.q: Name three input checks that catch a silently broken feature pipeline.
questions.a: The age of each feature table, with an alert if it stops updating; the share of requests where each feature is missing or at its default; and logged serving values compared with training values for the same examples.
